name: Milk Chocolate
lede: Milk Chocolate is a warm mid-brown named for the candy bar, and one of the most common colors in our painting archive even though chocolate itself reached Europe only in the 1500s.

sections.title: A candy-bar brown
sections.body:
Our library records Milk Chocolate only from the xkcd 2010 crowd survey, so its coining is undocumented beyond that, but the word *chocolate* as a color term is older: it entered English in the early 1700s, soon after drinking chocolate reached fashionable Europe [1][2]. The hex #7F4E1E measures lightness 38 and chroma 39 in LCH, lighter and less red than plain [[chocolate|Chocolate]] itself [1].

Its nearest named neighbors are [[milk-chocolate|Medium Brown]], 3.6 CIEDE2000 units away, and [[russet|Russet]], 3.8 units away, both read by the graph as almost the same color; plain [[chocolate|Chocolate]] sits a little further off at 5.1, redder and more vivid [3]. The color's own namesake plant is [[flower:chocolate|cacao]], whose raw beans are pale and mottled, not brown; the dark color only appears once they are roasted and fermented [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This brown is one of the most common colors in our archive, found in 2,929 of 23,781 paintings, 12.32%, as photographed, more common than 93% of the named colors here [5]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 98 of 945 paintings, present in 10.4% of paintings from that century, 1.9 times the archive's overall rate, and it most often plays an accent inside a painting [5]. Peter Paul Rubens carries it in 9 of his 46 works, 3.1 times the baseline, and it shares canvases with [[caramel|Caramel]] and [[seal-brown|Seal Brown]] more than chance would predict [5]. The earliest matching painting in our set is dated the year 1000, long before cacao reached Europe, which only shows that an aged, varnished brown can resemble this hue by chance, not that any medieval painter used chocolate, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [5].
